title: Mexico Meets Minimum Annual Water Delivery to the US Despite Extreme Drought
author: Arturo Sánchez Jiménez
content:
_This article by[Arturo Sánchez
Jiménez](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Arturo%20S%C3%A1nchez%20Jim%C3%A9nez)
originally appeared in the [October 24, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/10/24/politica/mexico-cumple-
con-entrega-minima-de-agua-del-rio-bravo-a-eu-pese-a-sequia-extrema), Mexico's
premier left wing daily newspaper._

**Mexico City**. Mexico met the minimum annual volume of water deliveries from
the Río Bravo (Rio Grande) to the United States as of this October 24, the end
of the first year of Cycle 37 under the 1944 Water Treaty, the Ministry of
Foreign Affairs (SRE) reported this Saturday, stressing that this was achieved
"in a context of extreme drought that affects the availability of water in the
region."

According to an SRE statement, the federal government coordinated inter-
institutional efforts to reach the goal set in the joint strategies announced
on February 3, 2026, and did so "**without putting at risk the human right to
water** , the consumption of communities, or food production, particularly in
the border region."

In Washington, US Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins confirmed in a
message on X that Mexico "met its commitment to deliver **at least 350,000
acre-feet of water** this year" (around 431 million cubic meters), although
she warned that "the work is not over," since continued deliveries and the
"repayment of the outstanding water debt" remain critical for farmers and
ranchers in South Texas.

The compliance comes after US President Donald Trump last year twice accused
Mexico of "violating" the 1944 Water Treaty and **demanded the immediate
delivery of water under the threat of imposing tariffs**.

For his part, Mexico's ambassador to the United States, Roberto Lazzeri, said
on social media that, despite the challenges posed by the prolonged drought,
"Mexico has met its commitment through dialogue and bilateral cooperation
guided by the leadership of President Claudia Sheinbaum, and based on the
principles of mutual respect, sovereignty, and shared responsibility."

> This progress shows what our two countries can achieve when they work
> together. We will continue building on these results to strengthen our
> cooperation.
>
> Roberto Lazzeri, Mexico's ambassador to the United States

In its statement, the Foreign Ministry emphasized that the actions undertaken
"reaffirm Mexico's commitment to complying with the 1944 Water Treaty and to
binational cooperation, based on the availability of the resource and the
hydrological conditions of the basin."

It also stressed that "access to water is a fundamental human right and a
priority for the government of Mexico," and therefore its management must
guarantee the well-being of the population and the continuity of essential
activities.

The SRE indicated that both countries maintain technical coordination to
strengthen the management of shared water resources and to develop
"predictable and sustainable solutions to the effects of extreme drought."

The federal government reiterated its willingness to continue working with the
United States to ensure compliance with the treaty, "for mutual benefit and
with full respect for national water sovereignty, the human right to water,
and the interests of Mexican communities."
